extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for examining patent applications under 35 U.S.C. 112 (written description, enablement, best mode, and claim definiteness), including when and how to make rejections and what evidence is required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assume best mode is disclosed unless evidence to the contrary
rubrics_metrics.description: The examiner should assume that the best mode is disclosed in the application, unless evidence is presented that is inconsistent with that assumption.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A best mode rejection is extremely rare in ex parte prosecution because information necessary to base such a rejection is rarely accessible to the examiner and is generally uncovered during inter partes proceedings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two-component best mode analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: A proper best mode analysis has two components: (A) Determine whether, at the time the application was filed, the inventor knew of a mode of practicing the claimed invention that the inventor considered to be better than any other (a subjective inquiry). (B) If (A) is true, compare what was known with what was disclosed — is the disclosure adequate to enable one skilled in the art to practice the best mode (an objective inquiry).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Only if the first (subjective) inquiry is answered affirmatively should the examiner analyze the second (objective) inquiry. A best mode rejection is proper only when (A) is affirmative and (B) is negative with reasons supporting nonenabling specification with respect to the best mode.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidence of concealment required for best mode rejection
rubrics_metrics.description: In determining adequacy of a best mode disclosure, only evidence of concealment (accidental or intentional) is to be considered; that evidence must tend to show that the quality of an applicant’s best mode disclosure is so poor as to effectively result in concealment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Citation of poor quality disclosure must support inference of concealment. Use sparingly; explain the basis (e.g., omissions, contradictions, or other record evidence) for concluding concealment.

rubrics_metrics.name: No best mode violation when missing information is readily known to skilled artisans
rubrics_metrics.description: The unintentional failure to disclose information that would be readily known to persons in the field of the invention does not violate the best mode requirement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: omission of commonly available motors or cranes, or methods that would be employed by those of ordinary skill, will not defeat best mode. Consider whether only routine skill is required to produce the omitted matter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Best mode cannot be satisfied solely by reference to prior art
rubrics_metrics.description: An inventor cannot meet the best mode requirement solely by reference to what was known in the prior art when the inventor knew a specific mode (e.g., a surface treatment) was necessary and did not disclose whether to use it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the inventor had knowledge that a particular mode or step was necessary for satisfactory performance and that mode was not disclosed (even if how to perform it was known in the art), this may support a best mode violation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Written description requirement (35 U.S.C. 112(a) / pre-AIA 1st paragraph)
rubrics_metrics.description: The specification shall contain a written description of the invention, and of the manner and process of making and using it, in such full, clear, concise, and exact terms as to enable any person skilled in the art to make and use the same, and shall set forth the best mode contemplated by the inventor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use form paragraph 7.30.01 (statement of statutory basis) as required; ensure any rejection under 112(a) is supported by record references and analysis demonstrating lack of written description or enablement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rejection for lack of written description — form paragraph 7.31.01
rubrics_metrics.description: Claim [1] rejected under 35 U.S.C. 112(a) ... as failing to comply with the written description requirement: the claim contains subject matter which was not described in the specification in such a way as to reasonably convey to one skilled in the art that the inventor had possession of the claimed invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Must be preceded by form paragraph 7.30.01 or 7.103. Examiner must identify the subject matter not properly described (page/line/drawings) and provide an explanation including any unresolved examiner questions that raise doubt as to possession.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rejection for lack of enablement — form paragraph 7.31.02
rubrics_metrics.description: Claim [1] rejected under 35 U.S.C. 112(a) ... as failing to comply with the enablement requirement: the claim contains subject matter which was not described in the specification in such a way as to enable one skilled in the art to make and/or use the invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Must be preceded by form paragraph 7.30.01 or 7.103. If problem is scope, use 7.31.03. In the explanation identify claimed subject matter not enabling and apply the Wands factors (In re Wands) as appropriate. Include any unresolved examiner questions relevant to enablement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope of enablement / commensurate scope rejection — form paragraph 7.31.03
rubrics_metrics.description: Claim [1] rejected ... because the specification, while being enabling for [2], does not reasonably provide enablement for [3]; the specification does not enable a person skilled in the art to [make/use] the invention commensurate in scope with these claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use when specification enables some embodiments but the claims are broader than the enabled disclosure. Identify the enabled subject matter and specific aspects of the claims not enabled; state whether the deficiency is make/use or both.

rubrics_metrics.name: Best mode requirement rejection — form paragraph 7.31.04
rubrics_metrics.description: Claim [1] rejected under 35 U.S.C. 112(a) ... because the best mode contemplated by the inventor ... has not been disclosed. Evidence of concealment of the best mode is based upon [2].
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Must be preceded by form paragraph 7.30.01 or 7.103. Insert specific basis for holding best mode concealed (e.g., disclosure quality effectively results in concealment). Use rarely; explain why the disclosure is so poor as to amount to concealment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope of enablement of a 'single means' claim — form paragraph 7.31.05
rubrics_metrics.description: Claim [1] rejected under 35 U.S.C. 112(a) ... because the claim purports to invoke 35 U.S.C. 112(f) (pre-AIA sixth paragraph) but fails to recite a combination of elements as required and thus cannot rely on the specification to provide the structure, material or acts to support the claimed function; the claim covers every conceivable means for achieving the stated function while the specification discloses at most only those means known to the inventor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use only when the claim recites a single element in means-plus-function format. This situation should be rare. Precede with form paragraph 7.30.01 or 7.103.

rubrics_metrics.name: Essential subject matter missing from claims (enablement) — form paragraph 7.33.01 / related guidance
rubrics_metrics.description: Claim [1] rejected ... as based on a disclosure which is not enabling: the disclosure does not enable one of ordinary skill in the art to practice the invention without [2], which is/are critical or essential to the practice of the invention but not included in the claim(s).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Must be preceded by form paragraph 7.30.01 or 7.103. In bracket 2 recite omitted subject matter and in bracket 3 give rationale for considering it critical/essential. Examiner shall cite statement/argument/date/drawing or other evidence showing applicant considered the feature essential.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two separate requirements under 35 U.S.C. 112(b) (pre-AIA 2nd paragraph)
rubrics_metrics.description: Two separate requirements: (A) the claims must set forth the subject matter that the inventor or a joint inventor regards as the invention; and (B) the claims must particularly point out and distinctly define the metes and bounds of the subject matter to be protected (definiteness).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The first requirement is subjective (dependent on inventor's view); the second is objective (evaluated for definiteness by a person of ordinary skill in the art). Examiners should determine whether rejection is for indefiniteness or for failure to claim what the inventor regards as the invention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidence to the contrary for what inventor regards as the invention
rubrics_metrics.description: A rejection based on failure to satisfy the requirement that claims set forth what the inventor regards as the invention is appropriate only where the inventor has stated, somewhere other than in the application as filed, that the invention is something different from what is defined by the claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evidence of contrary inventor view may be found in contentions or admissions in briefs, remarks, or affidavits (37 CFR 1.132). The content of the specification is not used as evidence that claim scope is inconsistent with what the inventor regards as the invention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Shift in claimed invention permitted during prosecution
rubrics_metrics.description: 35 U.S.C. 112(b) does not prohibit the inventor from changing what the inventor regards as the invention during the pendency of the application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Continuation practice and claim shifts are permissible; claims in a continuation directed to subject matter not regarded as part of the invention in the parent may still receive the parent filing date if conditions met (case citations provided).

rubrics_metrics.name: Unclaimed essential matter — multi-section rejection guidance
rubrics_metrics.description: Omitted matter described as essential in the specification may support rejection under 35 U.S.C. 112(a) (enablement or written description) or under 35 U.S.C. 112(b) (indefiniteness or failure to claim inventor-regarded invention), depending on facts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Essential matter may include missing elements, steps, or necessary structural cooperative relationships. If claim omits matter necessary to practice the invention, follow MPEP §§ 2163 and 2164 guidance. Features described as preferred or illustrative are not necessarily critical or essential.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims must particularly point out and distinctly claim the invention (definiteness)
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims must be definite so the public is informed of the boundaries of protected subject matter; claims that do not meet this standard must be rejected under 35 U.S.C. 112(b) as indefinite.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Indefiniteness rejections must clearly identify the language causing indefiniteness and thoroughly explain the reasoning. The primary purpose is public notice; the secondary purpose is to identify what the inventor regards as the invention for patentability and 112(a) analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim interpretation principle — applicants as their own lexicographers
rubrics_metrics.description: Applicants may define in the claims what the inventor regards as the invention in whatever terms they choose so long as any special meaning assigned to a term is clearly set forth in the specification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applicants may use functional language, alternative expressions, negative limitations, etc. A claim may not be rejected solely because of the type of language used to define subject matter. Where a special definition is used, it must be clearly in the specification as filed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Broadest reasonable interpretation (BRI) during examination
rubrics_metrics.description: During examination, a claim must be given its broadest reasonable interpretation consistent with the specification as it would be interpreted by one of ordinary skill in the art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: BRI is used because applicants can amend claims during prosecution; give claim terms their plain meaning unless inconsistent with the specification. Consider ordinary and customary meaning at time of the invention, using claims, specification, drawings, and prior art as evidence. Avoid importing limitations from the specification absent clear disclaimer.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plain meaning, specification as glossary, and limits on importing embodiments
rubrics_metrics.description: Under BRI, words of the claim must be given their plain meaning unless inconsistent with the specification. The best source for determining meaning is the specification; however, limitations drawn solely from the preferred embodiment should not be imported absent clear disclaimer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If an Office action used plain meaning and applicant claims a special definition, the applicant must point to where the specification as filed provides a clear and intentional special definition. An applicant may not add special definitions or disavowal after filing; may only point to what was in the specification as filed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Determine whether claim limitations invoke 35 U.S.C. 112(f) (pre-AIA sixth paragraph)
rubrics_metrics.description: For each claim limitation, determine whether it invokes 35 U.S.C. 112(f) / pre-AIA sixth paragraph (means-plus-function treatment).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a limitation invokes 112(f), evaluate whether the claim recites sufficient structure/elements or improperly attempts to rely on the specification to supply structure for a broad function-only claim; use 7.31.05 guidance when a single means element is present.
